**Bug — `st.data_editor` `NumberColumn` cell commits mid‑IME‑composition.** When a CJK IME is composing in a `NumberColumn` cell editor, the **Enter that confirms the IME composition** (fired with `KeyboardEvent.isComposing === true`) is also treated as "commit cell + move down", so the editor closes after the first digit and multi‑digit entry is impossible. This is the classic IME pitfall — the same class of bug previously fixed for `st.chat_input` in #6988.

**Root cause (candidate):** the cell overlay editor's key handler in the bundled `@glideapps/glide-data-grid` (`internal/data-grid-overlay-editor/…/data-grid-overlay-editor.tsx`, `onKeyDown`) commits on `event.key === "Enter" && !event.shiftKey` **without checking `event.nativeEvent.isComposing`**. Streamlit already has an IME‑safe guard for exactly this (`frontend/lib/src/util/inputUtils.ts` → `isEnterKeyPressed`, which returns `false` when `nativeEvent.isComposing`), but the dataframe/data‑editor overlay path does not go through it. The fix is to add the `isComposing` guard to the overlay editor's Enter/Tab commit.

**Repro confirmed:** with the code sample above, opening a `NumberColumn` cell, composing `1`, then pressing Enter to confirm the composition commits `1` and closes the editor (reproduced here on 1.59.0; the reporter additionally observes it on 1.60.0).

**Note on the regression window:** the bundled `@glideapps/glide-data-grid` version (`6.0.4-alpha24`), `NumberColumn.ts`, and the rendered overlay `<input type="text" inputmode="numeric">` are all **identical** between `1.58.0` and `1.59.0`, and an automated CDP reproduction (dispatching Enter with `isComposing = true`) commits the cell on **both** versions. So the mechanism above is confirmed, but the exact `1.58 → 1.59` behavioral difference the reporter observed could not be isolated via synthetic IME events — it may live in a subtler change among the ~250 commits in that window (focus/re‑render/event‑propagation timing around the overlay) or in a real‑IME nuance the synthetic events don't capture. Recommend verifying with a real macOS CJK IME and, if the version delta matters for the fix, `git bisect 1.58.0..1.59.0` with the provided repro.

### Related Issues

- **#6988** — *st.chat_input element does not behave as expected for Japanese input* (closed). Same root cause class (Enter during IME composition mis‑handled); the `isComposing` guard added there is the pattern to reuse here.

### Triage summary

This is a confirmed-looking layout **regression** in the new (`react-aria-components`) `st.selectbox`/ComboBox introduced in 1.59. When a selectbox sits near the bottom of the **sidebar**, its dropdown opens downward and overflows past the viewport instead of flipping up as it did in 1.58.

**Likely root cause:** the dropdown is positioned via Floating UI, but flipping is explicitly disabled inside the sidebar. In `frontend/lib/src/components/shared/Dropdown/Selectbox.tsx` the positioning hook is called with:

```tsx
const { refs, floatingStyles } = useFloatingOverlay({
  open: true,
  placement: "bottom-start",
  offsetPx: convertRemToPx(theme.spacing.twoXS),
  flipOptions: isInSidebar ? false : undefined, // <-- disables flip in the sidebar
  matchTriggerWidth: true,
})
```

In `useFloatingOverlay` (`frontend/lib/src/hooks/useFloatingOverlay.ts`), `flipOptions === false` drops the `flip()` middleware entirely, so the popover can no longer flip to `top` when there isn't enough space below — it just opens downward and gets clipped. This matches the reporter's DOM observation that in 1.59 the listbox renders inside `[data-testid="stSidebar"]` (which is `position: relative`) rather than at the document root as a sibling of `#portal` like in 1.58. This flip-disabling was added in the Floating UI scroll-tracking change (#15638); it was presumably meant to avoid the popover escaping the sidebar's bounds (the BaseWeb `Multiselect` uses the analogous `ignoreBoundary: isInSidebar`), but it also unintentionally removed the upward-flip behavior. A fix likely needs to keep flip enabled while constraining/shifting the popover against the viewport rather than fully disabling `flipOptions` in the sidebar.

### Related Issues

- [#12260 – Regression: Selectbox/Multiselect keyboard focus not activating on mobile](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12260): Another regression in the same widgets tied to the `react-aria` ComboBox rewrite — useful as a sibling regression from the same migration.
- [#12865 – Fullscreen menu partially hidden in fixed height containers](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12865): Same class of bug — an overlay/menu getting clipped by a relatively-positioned/overflow-constrained container's bounds instead of being viewport-aware.
- [#9340 – Popover is truncated when app is embedded](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9340): Also an overlay positioning/clipping problem where the popover isn't rendered relative to the viewport; related conceptually rather than a duplicate.

This is a confirmed frontend bug in the `st.expander` (and, via the same shared code path, `st.status`) open/close height animation. After a rapid sequence of expands/collapses, an expander can be left "permanently" clipped — showing a stale fixed height with the tail of its content cut off and unreachable until a rerun/reload replaces the element.

**Root cause (verified against `develop`):** The height animation locks the `<details>` element before animating by setting inline `height: <px>` and `overflow: hidden`, and relies on the Web Animations API `finish` event to clear those inline styles. In `frontend/lib/src/components/elements/Expander/animateHeight.ts`, the `finish` listener clears `element.style.height`/`overflow`, but the `cancel` listener intentionally does **not** (comment: "DON'T clean up on cancel - caller will set new styles"). `cancelAnimation()` in `useDetailsAnimation.ts` likewise only cancels and nulls the ref without clearing styles. This is safe *only if* a cancel is always followed by a new animation that eventually finishes. That assumption breaks when a cancel has no successor — e.g. the debounced `ResizeObserver` callback hits an early-return guard (`!details.open` / `!isOpenRef.current`) or the height delta is under `RESIZE_THRESHOLD_PX` (5px), the deliberate `contentHeight === 0` lock in the open path never gets healed by a ResizeObserver tick, or unmount cleanup. In those cases the inline `height`/`overflow` lock persists, clipping the content. `StyledDetails` in `styled-components.ts` sets no `height`/`overflow` of its own, so any inline `overflow: hidden` observed at rest on the `<details>` is confirmed residue from this cleanup gap. The reporter's analysis and suggested fix (clear inline styles on cancel / in `cancelAnimation()`, since callers already re-lock synchronously) are accurate and align with the code. Marked as a regression since this behavior was introduced with the newer WAAPI-based expander animation (`useDetailsAnimation`, #13933).

### Related Issues

- [#12859](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12859) — `st.expander` fails to display `st.pdf` when initialized collapsed. Closely related: content in an expander not rendering at full/correct height depending on collapsed/expanded state and layout timing, likely touching the same open-path height/ResizeObserver logic.
- [#7223](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7223) — Script reruns cause elements in expanded `st.status` containers to appear as grey artefacts prior to their animation. Related because `st.status` renders through the same `Expander` component and shares the `useDetailsAnimation` height-animation code path.
- [#8239](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8239) — `st.tabs` & `st.expander` — improve handling of frontend state/mount. Related area: frontend state/lifecycle handling of the expander, where interrupted animations and unmount cleanup interact.

This issue reports that `st.plotly_chart` with `on_select` enabled doesn't return any selection data for `px.imshow` (image show) or heatmap chart types. When users click on heatmap pixels or draw rectangle selections, the returned selection object remains empty.

**Root Cause Analysis:** This is a limitation stemming from how Plotly.js handles selection events for heatmap/image trace types. Looking at the frontend code in `PlotlyChart.tsx` and `utils.ts`, Streamlit relies on Plotly's `onSelected` event to capture selection data. However, Plotly.js doesn't fire the standard `plotly_selected` event for heatmap and image trace types (which `px.imshow` uses internally). These chart types don't support the same `selectedpoints` mechanism that scatter, bar, and other chart types do. To support this, Streamlit would need to implement custom handling using Plotly's `plotly_click` event for point selection or `plotly_relayout` callbacks for shape/rectangle selection on these specific chart types.

### Related Issues

- **#8933 - [Chart Selection not working on all plotly charts (e.g. Sankey; +heatmap/imshow)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8933)**: This is essentially a duplicate issue covering the same problem for heatmap/imshow and also Sankey diagrams. The root cause is identical - Plotly.js doesn't support standard selection events for these chart types.

- **#9001 - [Returning data from plot interactions doesn't work with Plotly Treemaps](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9001)**: Same underlying limitation affecting Treemap charts. The `on_select` feature doesn't work because Plotly.js doesn't emit selection events for this chart type.

- **#8824 - [plotly_chart support for click event](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8824)**: Related feature request asking for click events (vs selection events) in `st.plotly_chart`. Implementing click event support could provide a workaround for chart types that don't support selection.

**Here are some thoughts / request for feedback on how it might work, would love input and responses from anyone!**

### Use cases?

Thinking about 3 main scenarios for this currently:
- **Long running compute in the same process:** This seems to be the same use case described in the original issue. Say I have a RAG pipeline and some documents being indexed to an in-memory vector store. I'd like to run it in a separate thread so the user can continue interacting.
- **Waiting for a slow database call:** I ran something in a connected database (or similar), such as kicking off a Task / sproc in Snowflake or storing some embeddings in an outside vector store. Would be nice if the app isn't stuck while waiting for that to complete.
- **Waiting for a webhook callback from an external service:** Maybe I submitted an async request to a third party API like Twilio, Stripe, etc and I'd like to notify the user when it completes. Whenever we add #439, it would support a callback webhook. But then I need to also async call back into the running user session to update the app when that happens.

Are there others folks have in mind?

### Requirements

Hi, I've found a way to combine threading & fragment to get a fairly responsive behavior. 

Note: the example below is just one way of using this technique; I have since moved to another more complicated variation, but this is the most straight forward one: (Thanks mainly to the SO answer, and what jcarroll showed me in another exchange.)

Hope the Streamlit team can package the 'run_in_thread' decorator up somehow.

```
import time
from functools import wraps
from threading import Thread

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

import streamlit as st
from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import add_script_run_ctx, get_script_run_ctx


## function wrapper
def run_in_thread(func):
    # per https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76472211/multithreading-for-streamlit-and-kite-connect
    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        thread = Thread(target=func, args=args, kwargs=kwargs)
        ctx = get_script_run_ctx()
        add_script_run_ctx(thread, ctx)
        thread.start()
    return wrapper


# this is a fn that takes time to complete, (e.g. database call, etc.)
# so we run it in a thread
@run_in_thread
def generate_data(x=1, sleep=2):  # example from j.carroll
    print('in generate data fn')
    time.sleep(sleep)  # simulating the delay
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        np.random.randn(5, 5) * x, columns=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
    )
    print(f'returning df after sleep.. len={len(df)}')
    st.session_state.df = df


LOAD_FREQ = 10
@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def update_data():
    print('in update data fn')
    load_timer = st.session_state.load_timer
    now = time.monotonic()
    if now > load_timer + LOAD_FREQ:
        # avoid generating data all the time
        print('update data now > timer + freq')
        st.session_state.load_timer = now
        generate_data()


@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def filter_data(min_idx):
    print('in filter data fn')
    df = st.session_state.df
    st.session_state.df_f = df[df.index >= min_idx].copy()


@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def draw_graph(graph_slot):
    print('in draw graph fn')
    df = st.session_state.df_f
    if df is not None:
        graph_slot.plotly_chart(px.bar(df))


def init_states():
    if 'df' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.df = pd.DataFrame()
        st.session_state.df_f = pd.DataFrame()
    if 'load_timer' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.load_timer = time.monotonic()


def main():
    init_states()
    "`generate_data()` runs in the background, so these widgets remain fully interactive"
    st.button("Button 1")
    st.slider("Random slider", 0, 100)

    min_idx = st.selectbox('min idx', range(0, 5))
    graph_slot = st.empty()

    update_data()
    filter_data(min_idx)
    draw_graph(graph_slot)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

```

Thanks everyone for the rich discussion here. 🙏 Over time this issue has become a catch-all for several *distinct* needs, and most of them now have clearer, dedicated homes. To keep the conversation focused and actionable, we're closing this in favor of the more specific issues below — please 👍 and continue in whichever one matches your use case:

- **Loading independent sections / data in parallel to speed up a page** → use `st.fragment(parallel=True)`. Independent sections run concurrently and render into reserved containers, so total load time is the slowest section rather than the sum. See [Run fragments in parallel](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/fragments#run-fragments-in-parallel) (and the [`st.fragment` API reference](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/execution-flow/st.fragment)).

- **Long-running or non-blocking background work** — e.g. kicking off a slow computation or database/API call, updating the app when it finishes, or cancelling in-flight work → **#6687** (background execution).

- **Reacting to external events / webhooks** — receiving external HTTP calls is now supported via custom routes on **`st.App`** (the ASGI/Starlette integration, #439, available since 1.53 and the default in 1.57; feedback in #13600). Pushing such an event into a running session to update the UI is tracked in **#6687**.

- **CPU-bound work / `multiprocessing` / `ProcessPoolExecutor`** → tracked separately in **#4788** and **#7851**.

A note on calling `st.*` from your own or a library's threads: this remains unsupported and is not thread-safe — elements can arrive in the UI in an unpredictable order. For concurrency that renders as part of your app, use parallel fragments (which render into reserved containers). For work whose result you want to surface when it finishes, follow **#6687** — getting a completed background task to update the UI (rather than polling for it) is part of what that issue covers.

If your specific need isn't captured by any of the above, please open a new issue so we can track it! Thanks again for all the input here! 🎈

**Two Ways to Fix**
We took one of these two steps to avoid this:

1. On pages where we used multiprocessing, we put this statement at the top of the page to avoid having child processes run Streamlit rendering code again

    ``` 
    if multiprocessing.current_process().name != "MainProcess":

    ```
2. We also moved some background functions that we passed to `ProcessPoolExecutor`'s `submit` function out of the page and into a separate module that has no Streamlit dependencies
    - This avoids loading Streamlit packages and pages when the function executes

Approach 1) may work well in general as a fix within Streamlit?

Hi @amanchaudhary-95 — thank you for the detailed bug report and for identifying the working patterns. I've done some investigation and can confirm this is a valid issue.

**What's happening:**
When st.write_stream receives an async generator, it creates a temporary event loop to convert it into a sync generator, then shuts that loop down. However, when your LangChain model is cached with @st.cache_resource, its internal HTTP client retains references to the original event loop. On the second run, it tries to reuse that closed loop, which leads to the error.

**Why your working cases succeed:**

Case 1 (sync + cache): No async event loop is involved, so nothing breaks.

Case 2 (async + no cache): The model is recreated each time, so it doesn't reuse a stale loop.

Your testing shows that the failure is isolated to the specific combination of @st.cache_resource and async generators (Case 3).

**Documentation gap:**
While the docs state that st.write_stream supports async generators, they don’t mention this edge case involving cached resources.

This looks like a legitimate bug — Streamlit likely needs better event loop isolation or reuse when caching async resources. In the meantime, your Cases 1 and 2 are solid workarounds.

import asyncio
import atexit
import logging
import threading
from typing import Any, Coroutine, TypeVar

import streamlit as st

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


async def startup():
    print("Do startup stuff like Setting up logging, Creating async API connections etc")
    print("Startup completed")


async def shutdown():
    print("Do shutdown stuff like closing async API connections etc")


@st.cache_resource  # <----- this is what makes it possible to keep an event loop alive across multiple script runs (CTA clicks).
def get_global_loop():
    """
    Returns a persistent asyncio loop running in a background thread.
    The loop will live across Streamlit reruns and only be cleaned up at shutdown.
    """
    loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()

    def run_loop():
        loop.create_task(startup())
        loop.run_forever()

    t = threading.Thread(target=run_loop, daemon=True)
    t.start()

    def stop_loop():
        try:
            fut = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(shutdown(), loop)
            fut.result(timeout=5)
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"[shutdown] Error during cleanup: {e}")
        loop.call_soon_threadsafe(loop.stop)

    atexit.register(stop_loop)

    return loop


T = TypeVar("T")


def run_in_app_loop(coro: Coroutine[Any, Any, T]) -> T:
    """Run an async coroutine in the global loop and return its result."""
    loop = get_global_loop()
    fut = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop)
    return fut.result()

@aj-jaiswal007 Thanks for the help, but this only works with `ainvoke` and not with `astream` or `astream_events`. I took inspiration from your code and modified it to work for all `async` functions.

```python

# app_runtime.py
import asyncio
import atexit
import threading
import inspect
from queue import Queue
import streamlit as st

@st.cache_resource  # keep event loop across reruns
def get_global_loop():
    """Return a persistent asyncio loop running in a background thread."""
    loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()

    def run_loop_forever(loop_to_run):
        asyncio.set_event_loop(loop_to_run)
        loop_to_run.run_forever()

    t = threading.Thread(target=run_loop_forever, args=(loop,), daemon=True)
    t.start()

    def stop_loop():
        loop.call_soon_threadsafe(loop.stop)

    atexit.register(stop_loop)
    return loop


def run_in_app_loop(coro_or_async_iter):
    """
    Run a coroutine or consume an async iterator on the global loop and yield results.
    - If given an async iterator/generator, collect items in the app loop and yield them.
    - If given a coroutine, run it and yield its result (prefers .content if present).
    """
    loop = get_global_loop()

    # Async iterator / async generator: stream items via a background producer and a thread-safe queue
    if inspect.isasyncgen(coro_or_async_iter) or hasattr(coro_or_async_iter, "__aiter__"):
        q: Queue = Queue()
        SENTINEL = object()

        async def _pump():
            try:
                async for item in coro_or_async_iter:
                    q.put(item)
            finally:
                q.put(SENTINEL)

        asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(_pump(), loop)

        yield from iter(q.get, SENTINEL)

    # Coroutine
    elif asyncio.iscoroutine(coro_or_async_iter):
        result = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro_or_async_iter, loop).result()
        yield getattr(result, "content", result)
```

This is a bug involving a conflict between `st.cache_resource`, `st.write_stream`, and async generators. The root cause is in `async_generator_to_sync` (in `type_util.py`), which creates a new event loop and closes it after each stream completes. When `@st.cache_resource` caches an async client (like LangChain's `ChatOllama`), that client retains a reference to the original event loop. On subsequent reruns, when a new event loop is created, the cached client still tries to use the old (now closed) event loop, resulting in `RuntimeError: Event loop is closed`.

The workaround patterns (sync streaming without cache, or async without cache) work because they avoid the mismatch between cached clients and closed event loops. A proper fix would require either reusing event loops across reruns or preventing async clients from being cached.

### Related Issues

- **#8488** - [Native asyncio support](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8488): The overarching enhancement request for proper async/await support in Streamlit. Implementing native asyncio would fundamentally solve this class of event loop issues.

- **#744** - [RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread error](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/744): A long-standing related bug about asyncio event loop handling in Streamlit's threading model. Both issues stem from the same fundamental problem of event loop lifecycle management.

- **#12323** - [Streamlit is incredibly slow at calling anything via OpenRouter's API](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12323): May be related to async handling issues with LLM API calls via `st.write_stream`, potentially involving similar event loop conflicts.

Hey @nishant-emburse,

Coincidentally, we're currently working on a project that will eventually enable users to configure pieces of the file uploader widget so that it can operate more smoothly in multi-instance deployments.  We've recently worked on several projects with a similar theme of making the Streamlit internals more configurable, but the piece we're missing before we'll be able to expose all of these things publicly is a more advanced config system. See this comment on a similar issue for more context: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5849#issuecomment-1510010145.

That being said, even once everything is available for public use, I'd probably still recommend relying on session affinity to get `st.file_uploader` to work as expected in most multi-instance deployments.

The difficulty with getting a widget like the file uploader to work correctly when there are several streamlit server instances (assuming no session affinity) is that the file upload, which happens via HTTP as sending large files via websocket comes with its own set of difficulties, may land on a different server than the one the browser has a websocket connection to. As a result of this, a solution would require either
1. Streamlit servers to be able to talk to each other to pass files around
    * This would require some nontrivial configuration outside of streamlit itself to enable service discovery. It also feels somewhat hacky
2. A way to upload files to a shared location (like AWS S3 or some other intermediary service) rather than directly to an individual streamlit server

@nblackrjc Agreed that I'd like to be able to retrieve values from st.session_state within the callable if possible, but here's a workaround that I figured I'd share in case it's helpful to you:

Rather than directly providing the `get_data` callable to `st.download_button`, make it into a closure and provide its factory function to the button instead. Inside the factory function, copy any st.session_state values you need into regular local variables. Then, in `get_data()`, use those variables instead of the session state variables.

The outer function `get_data_factory()` is ran each time `st.download_button()` is created. However, since it returns a callable, the inner function `get_data()` isn't ran until the button is clicked. Thanks to Streamlit's execution model, assigning the `st.session_state` values to a local variable within the factory function should be functionally equivalent to being able to use the session_state values directly (unless you're changing the session state in a fragment that doesn't contain the download button, in which case the button won’t refresh and rebuild the closure).

```python
import streamlit as st

st.session_state['counter'] = 10

def get_data_factory() -> callable:
    def get_data():
        export_data = counter
        return str(export_data)
    counter=st.session_state['counter']
    return get_data

st.write(f"Counter value: {st.session_state['counter']}")
st.download_button(
    label="Download Counter",
    data=get_data_factory(),
    file_name="counter.txt",
)
```

This is a **feature request** (enhancement) to make `st.session_state` (and Streamlit commands) accessible inside the deferred-download callable that was added to `st.download_button` in 1.52 (#12942). Today the callable can't read session state, which limits the deferred-download feature when the data to export is derived from state.

The root cause is architectural rather than a bug: the deferred callable is registered via `media_file_mgr.add_deferred(...)` and only executed later, on demand, when the user clicks the button. Execution happens in `DeferredFileHandler.handle` (`lib/streamlit/runtime/backend_operation_handler.py`), which runs the callable on a separate worker thread via `asyncio.to_thread(...execute_deferred, file_id)`. Because `st.session_state` and other `st.*` commands resolve through the thread-local `ScriptRunContext`, and that context is not attached to the worker thread, the callable sees a "missing ScriptRunContext" warning and can't reach session state. Supporting this would require propagating the originating session's `ScriptRunContext` (or a scoped, read-only session-state snapshot) into the deferred execution thread. As multiple commenters note, the community workaround is a closure/factory that captures the needed session-state values into locals before the button is created.

### Related Issues

- **[#5053 — [Coming soon] Deferred data for download button](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5053)**: The original feature request that led to the deferred-download callable. This issue is a direct follow-up asking to extend that same feature so the callable can access session state.
- **[#12051 — missing ScriptRunContext! in ThreadPoolExecutor](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12051)**: Same underlying limitation — code running on a separate thread loses the `ScriptRunContext`, so session state and `st.*` commands are unavailable. Resolving context propagation to worker threads would address both.

##PR 

https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16009

## changes

Fixes the 1.59.0 regression where `st.selectbox` fuzzy search only matched contiguous substrings.

Since the BaseWeb → react-aria `ComboBox` migration (#15438), RAC applied its own default `contains` text filter on top of Streamlit's `fuzzyFilterSelectOptions` result, so the visible list was the intersection (substring-only). Streamlit's fuzzy matcher was still correct in isolation.

The fix passes a no-op `defaultFilter` to `<ComboBox>` so Streamlit's own filter (fuzzy / contains / prefix / none) is authoritative and the already-filtered `displayOptions` reach the ListBox unchanged. Per the [React Aria docs](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/ComboBox.html#custom-filtering), `defaultFilter` is the documented way to override the built-in filter.

Restores 1.58.0 behavior:

| Type | Dropdown |
| --- | --- |
| `ape` | `Grape`, `Apple` |
| `aple` | `Apple` |
| `rp` | `Grape` |

This is the default behavior on how arrow (what we use for dataframe serialization) handles `dict` values. It is also quite tricky to build a workaround for this. But I think we could eventually improve support for dict if there is enough interest for this enhancement. In the meantime, the workaround would be to convert the columns containing `dict` values to string before putting it into `st.dataframe`, e.g.:
`df["c"] = df["c"].astype("string")`

A bit more technical details on this: Arrow includes all of the dict variables that appear in the column in every individual cell. In the case above, we get the following information when deserializing from arrow: `{'s': None, 'y': None, 'q': None, 'r': ''}`. So, we can either choose to show `{'s': None, 'y': None, 'q': None, 'r': ''}` or to ignore all `None` values: `{'r': ''}`. Currently, we ignore all `None` values.

## Update 

The packaging use case is now supported via `st.App.run()` (added in #15563 and available since Streamlit 1.59.0), although `streamlit run <console-script>` itself still requires a Python-file target.

A package can expose a console script whose entry point does:

```python
from pathlib import Path
import streamlit as st

def main() -> None:
    st.App(Path(__file__).with_name("dashboard.py")).run()
```

Using an absolute package path is important because the generated console-script executable lives in the virtual environment's `bin` directory.

## Update

Streamlit 1.59+ will have a `submit_mode` parameter for `st.chat_input` that controls widget behavior after submission while the script is running:

- "submit" (default): The widget remains fully enabled after submission. Users can submit new messages while the script is running (existing behavior).
- "disable": The widget is automatically disabled after submission and re-enabled when the run completes. This prevents users from interrupting ongoing operations like LLM streaming.
- "stop": The submit button transforms into a stop button while the script runs, allowing users to halt execution (like the app's "Stop" button). The text area is disabled during the run.

1. use session state to control the input state, and get the input value
2. move everything into the **on_submit** callback, DO NOT use *st.chat_message("user").write(...)* in it, or will write dup items.

```python

if "disabled" not in st.session_state:

    st.session_state.disabled = True

    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": st.session_state.prompt})

if prompt := st.chat_input("You question here", on_submit=on_submit, disabled=st.session_state.disabled, key="prompt"):

):

Currently using the following workaround for this - 

1. Don't use keys. Instead, store the initial value inside the session state, and update the state manually.

2. If the widget goes out of view, make sure the initial values are up to date  

```python
from time import sleep
from streamlit.runtime.state import get_session_state
import streamlit as st

init_key = "__init_values__"


def main():
    view = st.radio("View", ["view1", "view2"])

    if view == "view1":
        text_input("Text1", key="text1")
        "☝️ Enter some text, then click on view2 above"
    elif view == "view2":
        "☝️ Now go back to view1 and see if your text is still there"

    st.write(st.session_state)


def text_input(label, key):
    if init_key not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state[init_key] = {}
    initial_values = st.session_state[init_key]
    try:
        value = initial_values[key]
    except KeyError:
        value = st.session_state.get(key, "")
        initial_values[key] = value

    value = st.text_input(label, value=value)

    st.session_state[key] = value
    return value


def ensure_hidden_widgets_loaded():
    new_session_state = get_session_state()._state._new_session_state
    for key, value in st.session_state.items():
        if key in new_session_state or key == init_key:
            continue
        st.session_state[init_key][key] = value


try:
    main()
finally:
    ensure_hidden_widgets_loaded()
```

I'm currently going through an exercise where I'm building a Streamlit proxy object which does the following:
* Intercept all calls to streamlit, and if the attribute is a callable, set the item in session_state using the same default logic that the widget would normally apply. For example, set multiselect box default to `[]` rather than `None`
* Pop value/default/index from args
* Wrap the callable with a function that sets the state item in our own state dictionary, only if the widget has a key defined and allows writing

Here's the bulk of the code:
```
def __getattr__(self, name):
        attr = getattr(self._original_st, name)

        if callable(attr):  # If the attribute is a function/method, wrap it

            def persist_widget_values(*args, **kwargs):
                logging.info(
                    f"Intercepted call to {name} with args={args}, kwargs={kwargs}"
                )

                # If a key exists, persist it!
                key = kwargs.get("key", None)
                if key:
                    # This lets us handle cases where widgets are called with only
                    # positional arguments, eg: st.radio("radio1", ["option1", "option2"])
                    # so we can correctly infer defaults
                    all_args_as_kwargs = inspect.getcallargs(attr, *args, **kwargs)
                    logging.debug(f"Re-wrote arguments to {all_args_as_kwargs}")
                    self._set_default_value(name, key, all_args_as_kwargs)

                    # We have to always pop the default/value setting kwargs to avoid WidgetStateDuplicationWarning
                    for k in ["value", "default", "index"]:
                        kwargs.pop(k, None)

                    if name not in UNCONTROLLABLE_WIDGETS: # List of widgets with writes_allowed = False
                        value = self._original_st.session_state[key]
                        self.items_to_persist[key] = value
                        logging.info(f"Interrupting cleanup for {key}")
                        self._original_st.session_state[key] = value
                return attr(
                    *args, **kwargs
                )  # Call the function with our updated kwargs

            return persist_widget_values
```



* Each time a page is initialized, restore state items which have been cleaned up:
```
def restore_persisted_items(self):
        """Restores state items which were linked to Streamlit widgets
        that are no longer displayed on the page. This allows us to keep
        tracking state items even if the current page doesn't use widgets
        with those keys
        """
        for key, value in self.items_to_persist.items():
            if key not in self._original_st.session_state:
                self._original_st.session_state[key] = value
```

I see what you mean, and I believe by default this is expected design when we do sparklines and charts in the dataframe. I don't believe our upstream implementation (Glide Data Grid) allows the ability to redefine the baseline yet.

I've marked this as an enhancement to see if others are interested in such a solution.

This issue reports that `st.column_config.BarChartColumn` renders the smallest value in a cell as an empty (zero-height) bar when the actual minimum is greater than zero, which looks misleading compared to `st.plotly_chart` with a fixed `y`-range.

This is actually the **documented default behavior**: `y_min`/`y_max` default to `None`, which the docstring defines as "every cell will use the minimum/maximum of its data." In `ChartColumn.ts` (`BaseChartColumn` → `getCell`), when `y_min` isn't set, `minValueDefault` falls back to the data's own `minValue`, so the smallest value maps to the chart's baseline and appears as an empty bar. A maintainer confirmed this is intended (sparkline) design and that the upstream Glide Data Grid rendering doesn't currently expose a configurable baseline, so it has been reclassified from a bug to an enhancement.

**Workaround:** pass an explicit baseline, e.g. `st.column_config.BarChartColumn("Values", y_min=0, y_max=10)`, to make bars render from zero like the Plotly example.

- [#9944](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9944) — "`y_min` and `y_max` not correctly honored in `*ChartColumn`" — closest match; also about the y-axis auto-scaling defaults of chart columns (values not clamped to configured limits). Same underlying scaling logic in `ChartColumn.ts`.
- [#12294](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12294) — "Color positive and negative bars in `st.column_config.BarChartColumn`..." — another enhancement request for how `BarChartColumn` renders/scales bars.
- [#12307](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12307) — "Horizontal bar chart column for `st.dataframe`" — related request for improved bar-chart column visualizations in dataframes.

This is a **feature request** for more advanced, dashboard-style layout primitives to build "map-centric" UIs (inspired by Google Travel and the JHU COVID map). It boils down to three layout capabilities: (1) nestable **horizontal scroll panes** (items added to the right, recommender-style), (2) nestable **vertical scroll panes** (items added to the bottom), and (3) **fixed, resizable split panes** pinned to the top/bottom/left/right of the window (e.g., a fixed HUD on top, an icon rail on the left, a map on the right, and a scrolling content area in the center). The core ask is fixed/pinned panels plus scrollable regions rather than the current top-to-bottom flow. This is squarely a layout enhancement; the map is just the motivating example, not the feature itself. Given the scope, most of this is likely better tracked via the more specific layout issues below (grid layouts, pinned/edge containers, and scrollable containers). Note the author stated they won't be monitoring the request.

### Related Issues

- [#11101 Grid layout](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11101) — Requests a native `st.grid` for complex dashboards with more control than columns. This is the closest umbrella match for building the map-centric dashboard arrangements described here.
- [#10722 Add a bottom layout container](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10722) — Requests a `st.bottom`-style container pinned to the main area. Directly related to request (3): fixed/edge-anchored panels (a step toward top/bottom/left/right pinned split panes).
- [#12476 Add `height` support to enable scrolling for more containers & elements](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12476) — Adds fixed-height, internally scrolling containers, which maps to the nestable vertical/horizontal scroll pane requests (1) and (2).

@Scoodood Thanks for the enhancement request. I was able to reproduce this [here](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-6978). Two important pieces of information on this: 
1. using `st.slider` will always be slower than the approach that directly combines it with a plotly slider since the `st.slider` approach requires a roundtrip from frontend -> backend -> frontend, while the Plotly slider only works on the frontend. 
2. You can just use the plotly slider also on a Streamlit frontend with the same speed, e.g.:

```python
import streamlit as st
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np


fig = go.Figure()
for step in np.arange(0, 5, 0.1):
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            visible=False,
            name="f = " + str(step),
            x=np.arange(0, 10, 0.01),
            y=np.sin(step * np.arange(0, 10, 0.01))))

fig.data[10].visible = True

# Create and add slider
steps = []
for i in range(len(fig.data)):
    step = dict(
        method="update",
        args=[              
            {"visible": [False] * len(fig.data)},
            {"title": "Slider switched to step: " + str(i)}],  
    )
    step["args"][0]["visible"][i] = True
    steps.append(step)

sliders = [dict(
    active=10,
    currentvalue={"prefix": "Frequency: "},
    pad={"t": 50},
    steps=steps
)]

fig.update_layout(
    sliders=sliders
)

st.plotly_chart(fig)
```

if audio:
    # Do something with `audio`

    # Update so that `audio is None` the next time around
    del st.session_state[audio_input_key]
    st.session_state.audio_input_key_counter += 1
```

- detect if the object implements __hash__ (eg frozen objects has a __hash__ impl and that's faster than a full dump) the bytes of the __hash__:int value could be fed to the md5 hasher.
- a special case could be handled for `def _to_bytes(...)` when a function is passed and hash the function's fully qualified name.

Note that when `pickle.dumps(pydantic_model)` is used things work fine.

This is easy enough to solve for Pydantic object specifically. I can send out a PR to address it soon.

For other types of objects I think we should research existing patterns (`__hash__`, `__reduce__`, etc.), and if nothing seems right then we'd introduce our own. In particular, we need to make sure Streamlit's hashing is stable across script reruns, which is a requirement many other hashing utilities fail.

In addition, we should also rethink how we're handling `__reduce__` today, which, as mentioned above, will break whenever the output includes reducer function.

@SRFU-NN unfortunately, as you already noted in your update, the contract for __hash__ is not deterministic on purpose with some built in types (eg to prevent timing attacks). You can also `@st.cache_data(persist="disk")` which would persist across sessions.

overall I do agree with @sfc-gh-tteixeira, more thought and design are needed. Either continue to support more of case pickle supports or just invoke __reduce__ directly rather than bypassing parts of the pickle logic or do something similar to what mojo has done to support hashing where GPUs might be involved - they've extended python's default __hash__ to support a second form `def __hash__(self, hasher):` that takes a hasher as a second argument to allow for more explicit control in certain cases.

Right now this is not at the top of our list, but if someone knowledgeable on existing patterns (`__hash__`, `__reduce__`, etc.) and on Streamlit's hasher wants to take a stab at making a proposal here, that would likely speed things up.

And by "proposal" I mean something in plain English (not necessarily with any accompanying code) talking about the alternatives, why they'd work / not work, and then describing a solution.

As of today, this is _expected behavior_, but I understand why this is confusing. We have adopted the mechanism that widgets that disappear from the page are removed from session state. There was a lot of confusion on what this means. The counter-bug we received is saying "Why does the widget continue to have a value after it disappeared?"

MPA demonstrates this problem by switching pages effectively removes widgets from session_state. There are two ways to think about the UX.

1.  MPA are "separate" apps. In this case, values set by session state are preserved, but values set by widget state (in session state) will disappear in the next run after the widget is removed. The idea is that each page is it's own self-functioning app, and therefore we expect the widget state to reset when going back to it.
2. MPA session state is all shared including widget state. This is what you are advocating as the expected behavior.

In the end, we identified (1) as the model to use and agreed on. I think the main reasoning is that to achieve (2) behavior, you simply save your widget state into session state as a separate variable. It's a little clunky though. I will leave this issue open to get feedback and ideas from the community.

Hi @kmcgrady,

Personally I've been aware of this for a long time and while I understand that this is a design decision, I have never understood the rationale for this particular choice.

One reason why I do not like it is that passing `key` to the widget is an explicit attempt to save the widget state in the session state. It is a very convenient syntactic sugar for associating widgets with explicit updates to `st.session_state` - or it would be, except it does not actually do that and it's not very upfront about that fact.

Personally, if the widget has been declared with the `key`, it usually means that I want to keep the state independently of whether the widget is currently displayed or not. Sometimes I do not care. And although I can certainly imagine valid reasons why someone would want the state to go away with the widget, I have never wanted it to, and if I did, I would prefer to explicitly clear the state anyway.

The fact that the saving is conditional on the widget being there and that fact is not very explicitly sign-posted in the description of the `key` parameter is very confusing to newcomers. I do not think it is much of an overstatement to say that on https://discuss.streamlit.io/ there is a thread about "why am I losing my widget state?" every other day.

For those of us who do know about it it results in code littered with callback functions which serve only the purpose of running the 'fake' widget session state into the 'real' persistent widget state.

I think the bottom line with this is that the way Streamlit state works now, there are three modes:

1. transient (normal widgets)
2. persistent (`st.session_state`)
3. persistent, but only sometimes (widget session state)

The existence of the third one is, in my opinion, not very useful.

Objectively, it is poorly documented. The [Session State API reference](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/api-reference/session-state) treats the two like as if they were the same thing:

>Every widget with a key is automatically added to Session State:

The [Multipage Apps](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/get-started/multipage-apps) site explicitly says:

>Pages share the same [st.session_state](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/session-state):

The linked page says:

>Session State provides the functionality to store variables across reruns. Widget state (i.e. the value of a widget) is also stored in a session.

>For simplicity, we have unified this information in one place. i.e. the Session State. This convenience feature makes it super easy to read or write to the widget's state anywhere in the app's code. Session State variables mirror the widget value using the key argument.

This hints at the fact that the two are different, but never properly explains the caveats of using the widget state. The only place that does is the [Advanced notes on widget behaviour](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/widget-semantics):

>If you don't call a widget function in a script run, we neither store the widget state nor render the widget. If you call a widget function with the same arguments later, Streamlit treats it as a new widget.

While updating the documentation to really drive home the real behavior could be one solution, I would argue that whoever wrote the documentation described how this process would work in an intuitive manner: *if you put the `key` on a widget, the state will be saved in `st.session.state`, which persists between pages*, and it's the real behavior that is counter-intuitive.

Closing this since it was implemented in https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/15645

Adds a keyword-only `persist_state=None | "page" | "session"` parameter to most widgets that preserves a keyed widget's value when it stops being rendered. Persistence is purely a server-side state decision.

- `None` (default): current behavior — value is lost when the widget isn't rendered or on a page switch.
- `"page"`: keep the value while the widget isn't rendered on the **same page**; drop it on a page switch (not restored on return, and never leaks to another page that reuses the key).
- `"session"`: keep the value for the whole session, including across page switches.

Hi @JunShern,

For videos that are not too heavy, I found using `matplotlib` in combination with Streamlit's `session_state` to control videoflow works excellently. Additionally, I can easily superpose lines, circles, and scatter from potential user input as I'm working with a `pyplot` object (which is super versatile), it has been very useful for my personal use-case.

```python
import time
import skvideo.io
import skvideo.datasets
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import streamlit as st


@st.cache()
def init_state():
    if 'frame' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.frame = 0
    if 'playing' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.playing = False


def toggle_play():
    st.session_state.playing = not st.session_state.playing
    st.session_state.frame -= 1


def reset():
    st.session_state.playing = False
    st.session_state.frame = 0


# Initialize state
init_state()

# Import video in format (T, W, H, C)
video = skvideo.io.vread('test.mp4')
framerate = 60.

# Display
display = plt.imshow(video[st.session_state.frame])
plt.axis('off')

player = st.pyplot(plt)

# Controls
_, lcenter, center, _, _ = st.columns(5)
lcenter.button('Reset', on_click=reset)
center.button('Play/Pause', on_click=toggle_play)

while st.session_state.playing:
    st.session_state.frame = (st.session_state.frame + 1) % video.shape[0]
    time.sleep(1. / framerate)
    display.set_data(video[st.session_state.frame])

    player.pyplot(plt)

```

This bug occurs when `st.date_input` is the first widget inside an `st.popover` or `st.dialog`. When the popover/dialog opens, it auto-focuses on the first focusable element (the date input field). The BaseWeb Datepicker component used by `st.date_input` is designed to open its calendar dropdown when the input receives focus, which creates the unintended UX of the calendar immediately appearing when the popover opens. This contrasts with `st.selectbox` which only opens on click, not focus.

**Root cause**: The combination of two behaviors: (1) popover/dialog auto-focus on first widget, and (2) BaseWeb Datepicker opening on focus. A fix could either modify the autofocus behavior in popover/dialog, or prevent `st.date_input` from opening on programmatic/initial focus (only on user click).

This issue reports that the `/_stcore/health` endpoint causes page refreshes/reruns in Docker and cloud deployments (AWS, Azure) when running long processes. The root cause is that the health endpoint returns plain text `"ok"` which the frontend previously attempted to parse as JSON, causing errors in certain deployment environments. Notably, the frontend code has since been updated (in `frontend/connection/src/utils.ts`) to properly handle both JSON and text responses by trying JSON parsing first and falling back to text. Users affected by this issue may benefit from upgrading to a newer Streamlit version where this fix is included. The issue also relates to timeout handling during health checks which can trigger reconnection attempts and page reruns.

### Related Issues

- **#7074** - [404 health check when navigating directly to a subpage](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7074): Related health check endpoint issue where navigating directly to multipage app subpages causes 404 errors on relative health check paths. Both issues involve health check URL/response handling in deployment scenarios.

- **#8901** - [Reconnect to existing sessions instead of creating new upon unclean websocket close](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8901): Related issue where websocket connection interruptions cause new sessions instead of reconnecting. Both issues result in similar user-facing symptoms (lost progress, page refreshes) during network/connection events.

- **#4715** - [Streamlit health check (/healthz) ignoring 302](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4715): Another health check endpoint issue where HTTP 302 redirects (from auth proxies) are treated as failures. Both issues involve health check behavior causing problems in proxy/cloud deployment environments.

This is a CSS styling bug related to checkbox/toggle margin handling inside nested layout containers. The issue occurs when checkboxes or toggles are placed inside a horizontal `st.container` that is itself inside an `st.column`. 

**Root Cause Analysis:** The bug originates in `frontend/lib/src/components/core/Block/styled-components.ts` (lines 166-171). When a column uses default vertical alignment (TOP), a CSS rule applies `marginTop: theme.spacing.sm` (0.5rem) to the first checkbox using the selector `& ${StyledElementContainer}:first-of-type > ${StyledCheckbox}`. However, when checkboxes are inside a horizontal container, the `:first-of-type` CSS selector only matches the first `StyledElementContainer` containing a checkbox within that container, causing only the first checkbox to receive the margin while others do not. This results in inconsistent vertical spacing between checkboxes in the same horizontal row.

### Related Issues

- **#10265** - Same author reported a very similar bug where the `:last-of-type` selector caused unexpected margins on the last checkbox. This is essentially the same underlying issue but manifesting differently with horizontal containers.

- **#12434** - Related alignment issue where padding on elements inside horizontal containers causes visual misalignment, showing a pattern of layout issues with horizontal containers.

- **#11207** - Related enhancement request for toggle widget layout control, indicating user needs around toggle/checkbox styling in containers.

This is a well-documented regression where the parent page's scroll position (`stMain.scrollTop`) resets to 0 after closing an `st.dialog` that was opened via a custom component's `setComponentValue`. The reporter identified two distinct regressions:

1. **v1.41.0** (Firefox-only, specific DOM shapes): Caused by commit `96241e1` which migrated iframe styles from global styles to per-component styled-components for `CustomComponent`. The new `StyledComponentIframe` toggles `display: "initial" | "none"` based on `componentReady`, which can cause layout recalculations that disturb scroll position when the iframe re-renders during a script rerun triggered by dialog close.

2. **v1.53.0** (all browsers, all component shapes): Likely compounded by changes to dialog identity handling (commit `5319def` — "Prevent `st.dialog` from showing elements from previous dialog") and the introduction of `TransientNode`/`ClearTransientNodesVisitor` which alter how the render tree is rebuilt during reruns. When the dialog closes and triggers a rerun, the combination of dialog node clearing and custom component iframe re-rendering causes the browser to reset `stMain`'s scroll position. Notably, Streamlit has no explicit scroll preservation logic for the main content area during reruns — scroll stability relies entirely on DOM stability, which these changes disrupted.

### Related Issues

- **#6953** — [Page automatically scrolls itself when interacting with widgets](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6953): Same symptom of unexpected scroll position jumps during rerun/re-render cycles, though triggered by native widgets rather than custom components + dialog.
- **#12716** — [Long dialog starts at the bottom](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12716): Related dialog scroll issue (dialog's *internal* scroll position), with an open fix PR [#14505](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14505) that adds `scrollTop` reset to the dialog container — different scroll surface but same dialog lifecycle area.
- **#10199** — [Page Reload on Cache Miss](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10199): Reports page scrolling to top during reruns triggered by cache expiration — same root symptom of scroll position loss during rerun, different trigger mechanism.

VegaFusion can operate in two modes:

### pre-transform
It can take a Vega spec and pre-evaluate the data transformations to produce a new Vega spec that can be rendered with the regular Vega/Vega-Embed JavaScript library (e.g. for the example of a histogram, the output Vega spec would contain an inline dataset with one row per histogram bin). This is the easiest to integrate since it doesn't require custom logic in the client, but since there's not ongoing connection between the client and the server, it's not as helpful for interactive charts that transform data in response to interactive selections.

This is the foundation that the VegaFusion mime renderer is built on: https://vegafusion.io/mime_renderer.html. In this case, the Vega-Lite to Vega compilation is handled in the Python kernel with [VlConvert](https://github.com/vega/vl-convert).

### live connection
It can maintain a live connection between the client and the server. This way selection events can trigger the re-evaluation of  data transformations, and examples like [linked histogram brushing](https://altair-viz.github.io/gallery/interactive_layered_crossfilter.html) can be rendered without ever sending the entire dataset to the browser.

This requires some custom code in the client, and is the foundation that the VegaFusion widget renderer is built on: https://vegafusion.io/widget_renderer.html.

In this case, the Vega-Lite to Vega compilation can happen in the browser before rendering.

### Streamlit
My thinking was that the pre-transform workflow would be an easier fit with streamlit, since I wasn't sure that it was possible to maintain a connection between the client and server that wouldn't trigger re-rendering the page.  This is what Ken and I started playing with.

The main obstacle we ran into was that streamlit assumes that a Vega-Lite spec is sent to the browser and performs some theming and customization on it before rendering.  Sending a Vega spec instead would require some customization of this logic to work on a Vega spec.  I think this is possible, just would take some working through.

Thanks for taking a look! And sharing the API sketches, I think it's great.

Our goal with `st.navigation`, especially with the initial release, is to cover the most common cases with an easy and straightforward API. I think we succeeded with that goal :)

For more complex patterns like you recommended, **the intended pattern today is to use `st.navigation(..., position="hidden")` to hide the default nav and then build what you want with `st.page_link` (or even custom components!)**

With that said, we did sketch out some ideas for an `st.Section` or `PageGroup` as you mentioned, which could have some more advanced functionality like being collapsible.

Definitely think it's worthwhile to assess how much community demand we have for those, to help with prioritization - so I'm glad we have this issue (and I think it's worth updating the top description with an update and the remaining gap, to help point new Streamlit developers in the right direction)

Just for expectation setting, I'll also say _most likely_ we will focus in some other areas for a while, and I think we would want to build a native top navigation before / alongside adding deeper native hierarchy support like this. So I'd guess the earliest the core development team would pick this up would be some time in 2025, unless we heard a huge swell of demand.

I continue to find that (for non-trivial apps) the barrier is always incompatibilities in the Python environment across platforms, or conflicting with existing installed components.

I think it is also worth bearing in mind that Electron installers aren't always straightforward, and each build needs to be signed and (for MacOS) notarised to have any chance of the operating system reacting well to it... and both Windows and Mac seem to be closing up on even allowing the user to choose to bypass these safety checks.

Anyway, based on my experience progress first needs to be made in ensuring reliable portability of the Python environments, interpreters, etc. Adding an Electron front-end should ultimately be possible.

Hey @Abdelgha-4, thanks for reporting the issue! I was able to reproduce it via this deployed app: https://issues.streamlit.app/?issue=gh-10025
The root cause seems to be that the mutable_status_container.py in the update function enqueues the message [here](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/elements/lib/mutable_status_container.py#L154), which is handled by the event handler in app_session.py [here](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/runtime/app_session.py#L658) instead of the delta_generator.py's `enqueue` message which would save it to the cache [here](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/delta_generator.py#L553). So the `status.update` is not itself enqueuing an element that is cached.
Since caching simply replays the messages, you should be able to change your code to the following which should not make a huge difference performance-wise:

```python
import time

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_data(show_spinner=False)
def show_data():
    st.write("Searching for data...")
    time.sleep(2)
    st.write("Found URL.")
    time.sleep(1)
    st.write("Downloading data...")
    time.sleep(1)


with st.status("Downloading data...", expanded=True) as status:
    show_data()
    status.update(label="Download complete!", state="complete", expanded=False)
```

I tried to see if `caching.save_block_message` would allow `status.update` to be cached, but there's a validation check for nested expander elements that gets hit when you replay the cache. Presumably this is because it can't tell (yet) that `status.update` is replacing itself rather than generating a new nested block. Fixing this will require some extra thought...

# Memory Leak Analysis in Streamlit Video Component

## Issue Description
The reported problem occurs when fast-forwarding a video, where memory usage multiplies with each seek operation, eventually causing the application to crash.

## Code Analysis

### Key Findings

1. **Primary Issue: Media File Management**
   - In `_marshall_av_media()`, every time media data is processed, it's added to the media file manager:
   ```python
   file_url = runtime.get_instance().media_file_mgr.add(
       data_or_filename, mimetype, coordinates
   )
   caching.save_media_data(data_or_filename, mimetype, coordinates)
   ```
   - This appears to be creating new entries in the media file manager with each interaction, without cleaning up previous entries.

2. **Memory Management Concerns**
   - The code saves media data both in the media file manager and in the cache
   - There's no visible cleanup mechanism for old media files
   - Each seek operation likely creates a new media file entry

3. **Problematic Implementation Pattern**
   - The current implementation treats each video seek operation as a new media file
   - This leads to duplicate storage of the same video file with different start times
   - The memory usage grows linearly with each seek operation

## Root Cause

The memory leak appears to stem from the combination of two factors:

1. Each seek operation triggers a new media file registration
2. Old media files are not being cleaned up from either:
   - The media file manager
   - The caching system

## Proposed Solution

1. **Media File Reuse**
   - Instead of creating new media file entries for each seek operation, reuse the existing media file URL
   - Only register the media file once and store its URL
   - Use URL parameters for seek operations instead of creating new media files

2. **Implementation Changes Needed**

```python
def marshall_video(coordinates, proto, data, mimetype="video/mp4", start_time=0, ...):
    # Add a flag to track if this is a seek operation
    is_seek_operation = hasattr(proto, 'original_url') and proto.original_url
    
    if is_seek_operation:
        # Reuse existing media URL and just update the start time
        proto.url = proto.original_url
    else:
        # Only create new media file entry for initial load
        if isinstance(data, str) and url_util.is_url(data):
            proto.url = data
        else:
            # Store original URL for future seek operations
            file_url = runtime.get_instance().media_file_mgr.add(
                data_or_filename, mimetype, coordinates
            )
            proto.original_url = file_url
            proto.url = file_url

    # Add start_time as URL parameter instead of creating new file
    if start_time > 0:
        proto.url = f"{proto.url}#t={start_time}"
```

3. **Cleanup Mechanism**
Add a cleanup mechanism in the media file manager:
```python
class MediaFileManager:
    def cleanup_old_files(self):
        # Implement cleanup of unused media files
        # Could be triggered periodically or when memory usage exceeds threshold
        pass
```

## Additional Recommendations

1. **Memory Monitoring**
   - Add memory usage monitoring to the media file manager
   - Implement automatic cleanup when memory usage exceeds thresholds

2. **Caching Strategy**
   - Review the caching strategy to prevent duplicate storage
   - Implement cache eviction policies

3. **Error Handling**
   - Add proper error handling for memory-related issues
   - Implement graceful degradation when memory limits are approached

4. **Documentation**
   - Update documentation to clarify memory usage patterns
   - Document any limitations on video seeking operations

These changes should significantly reduce memory usage during video seeking operations while maintaining functionality.

I see the problem here, and I'm not _entirely_ sure that it qualifies as a "bug".

The way that `unittest.mock.patch` works is that it parses your module string (in this case `"foo.dialog_func"`) to extract the module name ("foo") and then loads that into python via some fancy import mechanics (the `importlib._bootstrap` section of your traceback) so that it can patch the name `"dialog_func"` within the "foo" `Module` object. 

Now if you're familiar with how python imports work, you may know that when you `import` something, it just _runs_ the entire contents of the module file. So when `patch` loads `foo`, the last thing it does is calls `dialog_func()` since that's the last line in `foo`. And because `dialog_func()` is a decorated function, it actually calls into streamlit internal code for dialogs before any of the streamlit context has been set up by `AppTest`.

Now, this is where my understanding of `DeltaGenerators` breaks down a bit; the `Dialog` object that's getting returned inside the streamlit code that wraps `dialog_func()` when you call it is not the `Dialog` object that it's supposed to be, for some reason, and it is missing that `.open()` method. I'm not sure why that isn't the case when the code is run inside an `AppTest` or `ScriptRunner` context, though -- the internals here are too spaghettified for me to have any hope of figuring that out.

------------

**tl;dr** your `patch` is causing your test to try to call a `st.dialog()`-decorated function _outside_ of the streamlit context, which is definitely a thing that's never going to be guaranteed to work. My recommendation to fix this is move your function definitions to a separate module (perhaps `foo_funcs.py`) where you can patch them without having to worry about the action of importing the module also executing any of the functions.

```python

# foo_funcs.py
import streamlit as st

@st.dialog("Test")
def dialog_func():
    st.write("Hello, world!")

def dummy_func():
    pass

# foo.py
import foo_funcs
foo_funcs.dialog_func()

# test_foo.py
from unittest.mock import patch

from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest


def test_foo():
    with patch("foo_funcs.dummy_func"):
        at = AppTest.from_file("foo.py").run()
        assert at.markdown[0].value == "Hello, world!"
```

### Triage summary

This is a confirmed **bug**: when the content of an `st.empty()` placeholder (or its `.container()`) is rewritten multiple times **within the same script run** and a later render produces **fewer** child elements at a given path than an earlier render, the extra elements are not removed and linger as "ghost" elements.

**Likely root cause (frontend render tree):** Stale-element removal is driven entirely by `scriptRunId`. In `AppRoot.addBlock` (`frontend/lib/src/render-tree/AppRoot.ts`), when a block at a delta path is replaced by a block of the same type, the new block **inherits the previous block's children** to preserve widget/React state. Incoming deltas overwrite children by index (`SetNodeByDeltaPathVisitor`), but if the new render has fewer children than before, the leftover inherited children are never overwritten. Because all of these writes happen in the *same* run, those leftover children carry the *current* `scriptRunId`, so `ClearStaleNodeVisitor`/`clearStaleNodes` — which only drops nodes whose `scriptRunId` differs from the current run — cannot tell them apart from fresh nodes and leaves them on screen. This matches @sfc-gh-dmatthews's observation ("we stale things from previous runs, but not when rewriting within an empty on the same run") and mirrors the special-case child-inheritance handling already added for dialogs (issue #10907, same code path). A community contributor (@charliec05) has indicated a fix along these lines is in progress.

- [#6063 — Clean-slate rendering](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6063): Enhancement requesting explicit control to clear old elements before re-rendering to avoid lingering "ghost" elements — the general form of the behavior gap behind this bug.
- [#10126 — `st.close()`/`st.end()` to remove stale elements](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10126): Requests a way to mark the end of a container's stream and remove trailing stale elements, closely related to the streaming/partial-render use case reported here.

# Solution 

I created an alternative version using a FastAPI local proxy but kept st.write_stream for Streamlit's UI. This completely solved the issue and performance became almost on par with using CLI and no Streamlit:

`Took 8.53s (via local proxy)`

I will stick with this as a workaround but I'm still curious why Streamlit itself has such poor performance.

## New streamlit_app.py:
```
import os
import time

import requests
import streamlit as st

PROXY_URL = os.environ.get("LOCAL_PROXY_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8000/stream")
DEFAULT_MODEL = "openai/gpt-5-nano"

if "messages" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.messages = []

for message in st.session_state.messages:
    with st.chat_message(message["role"]):
        st.markdown(message["content"])

model = st.sidebar.text_input("Model", value=DEFAULT_MODEL)

if prompt := st.chat_input("Ask anything"):
    st.chat_message("user").markdown(prompt)
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": prompt})

    with st.chat_message("assistant"):
        start_time = time.perf_counter()
        # Stream plain text from the local proxy
        try:
            with requests.get(
                PROXY_URL,
                params={"prompt": prompt, "model": model},
                stream=True,
                timeout=(10, 60),
            ) as r:
                if r.status_code != 200:
                    st.error(f"Proxy error {r.status_code}: {r.text[:500]}")
                    response = ""
                else:
                    response = st.write_stream(
                        (
                            chunk
                            for chunk in r.iter_content(
                                chunk_size=1024, decode_unicode=True
                            )
                            if chunk
                        )
                    )
        except Exception as exc:
            st.error(f"Proxy request failed: {exc}")
            response = ""
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start_time
        st.caption(f"Took {elapsed:.2f}s (via local proxy)")
    st.session_state.messages.append(
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": f"{response}",
        }
    )
```

## New proxy.py:
```
import os

import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse, PlainTextResponse, StreamingResponse

# Load from .env if present
load_dotenv()
OPENROUTER_API_KEY = os.environ.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY", "")
OPENROUTER_URL = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions"
HTTP_HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {OPENROUTER_API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}

SESSION = requests.Session()

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/health")
def health() -> PlainTextResponse:
    return PlainTextResponse("ok")


@app.get("/stream")
def stream(prompt: str, model: str):
    if not OPENROUTER_API_KEY:
        return JSONResponse({"error": "Missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY"}, status_code=500)
    payload = {
        "model": model,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        "stream": True,
    }
    try:
        r = SESSION.post(
            OPENROUTER_URL,
            headers=HTTP_HEADERS,
            json=payload,
            stream=True,
            timeout=(10, 60),
        )
    except Exception as exc:
        return JSONResponse({"error": f"request failed: {exc}"}, status_code=502)

    if r.status_code != 200:
        return JSONResponse({"error": r.text, "status": r.status_code}, status_code=502)

    def gen():
        for raw_line in r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
            if not raw_line:
                continue
            line = raw_line.strip()
            if not line.startswith("data: "):
                continue
            data = line[6:]
            if data == "[DONE]":
                return
            # Transform OpenRouter JSON SSE into plain text chunks for the client
            try:
                obj = __import__("json").loads(data)
                content = obj["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content")
                if content:
                    yield content
            except Exception:
                # Ignore non-content events
                continue

    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/plain")
```

Thanks for the detailed report, @zcabaal — I can reproduce this on 1.59.2 and it's still the behavior on `develop`.

This is actually **working as designed** rather than a bug in the wiring: `bind="query-params"` deliberately keeps URLs clean by only serializing *non-default* values. When a bound widget's value equals its default (`index=0` for `selectbox`, `default=["Option1"]` for `multiselect`), the param is intentionally removed from the URL — both on first render and when you re-select the default. This is enforced consistently on the frontend and backend.

That said, your use case is a good one that the current design doesn't cover: in **dynamic apps where the options or defaults can change**, a shared URL that omitted the default won't reproduce the same selection later. Forcing the value into the URL regardless of the default is a reasonable capability we don't offer today — so I'm reframing this as an **enhancement** (an opt-in to always serialize bound values), which the team can weigh in on.

In the meantime, you can get the "always include the value" behavior by syncing manually instead of using `bind`:

```python
options = ["Option1", "Option2", "Option3"]
opt = st.selectbox(
    "Choose an option:",
    options,
    index=options.index(st.query_params.get("key1", "Option1")),
    key="key1",
)
st.query_params["key1"] = opt  # written even when it's the default
```

This writes the value on every run regardless of whether it matches the default, so shared URLs stay stable even if the defaults change.

### Issue analysis

This is a **bug / upstream-dependency regression**. Streamlit's `lib/pyproject.toml` currently declares `websockets>=12.0.0,<17`, which still allows `websockets` to resolve to **16.1** (released 2026-07-09). That release "Blocked non-ASCII values in Headers", so any WebSocket handshake carrying a UTF-8 header value is now rejected.

Streamlit doesn't import `websockets` directly — it's used as **uvicorn's WebSocket protocol implementation** (`ws="websockets-sansio"` for uvicorn ≥ 0.44.0, else `"auto"`), configured in `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_server.py` (`_get_websocket_protocol`). The handshake header parsing therefore happens inside the `websockets` layer. When a reverse proxy / forward-auth layer (e.g. Authelia injecting a `Remote-Name` with accented or non-Latin characters) forwards a non-ASCII header, `websockets` 16.1 rejects it and the `/_stcore/stream` handshake fails, leaving the app stuck on "Please wait...".

**Likely fixes** (as the reporter notes): tighten the constraint to exclude the broken range (e.g. `websockets>=12.0.0,<16.1` or skip 16.1) and/or sanitize/percent-encode forwarded header values before they reach the `websockets` layer. Note the concern is valid even with the existing `<17` cap, since 16.1 falls within it.

### Related Issues

- [#8799](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8799) — "WebSocket header HTTP_SEC_WEBSOCKET_PROTOCOL value changed ... which gives connection error" (closed). Directly referenced by this issue; same failure class of a WebSocket handshake failing due to a header value.
- [#8188](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8188) — "Unnecessary failover on /_stcore/stream". Same symptom/deployment context: the `/_stcore/stream` WebSocket hangs/fails when running behind a reverse proxy.
- [#12108](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12108) — "Frequent websocket connection drops ...". Same pattern of an upstream WebSocket-layer dependency change (Tornado 6.5.1) breaking WebSocket connectivity for users behind proxies/Nginx.
